title: Fluently Add and Subtract Multi-Digit Whole Numbers
arc: The market ledger — sealed bids, combined receipts, the council reserve, the warehouse expansion, water damage, and the audit seal.
sources: NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data), grades 3–5 progression: quantitative approaches to collecting data, multiple trials, tables and graphical displays, and analysis of data with mathematics — nextgenscience.org, Appendix F

Data Nuggets (MSU KBS LTER, NSF DRK-12 funded): free K–16 activities built on authentic data from real scientific research; students follow the process of science — prediction, visualizing, interpreting, evidence-based claims, new questions — datanuggets.org

Playground Architect PBL (Magicore Learning): grade-4 STEM project-based learning explicitly aligned to CCSS 4.NBT.B.4 — model making, measurement, and cost totals with multi-digit addition and subtraction
Schoolyard SITES (UNH Cooperative Extension): real schoolyard science investigations for grades 2–5 that generate measurement data for classroom analysis

ISTE, 'Classroom AI Projects' (K-12 project guide): students evaluate AI — comparing assistants, using AI to solve problems — mapped to Knowledge Constructor 3.b (evaluate the accuracy, perspective, credibility and relevance of information) and Innovative Designer 4.a (a deliberate design process) — cdn.iste.org AIGDSE_1120

NSTA, 'AI in the Science Classroom' (Sept 2024): the responsible-use rule adopted here — 'Student use of AI should support learning, not replace it… Work generated by AI is not considered the student's own work' — nsta.org/blog/ai-science-classroom

AI4K12 (AAAI + CSTA, NSF DRL-1846073), Five Big Ideas in AI, grades 3–5 band: 'compare answers from two assistants' and ask 'what might the assistant not know? who is missing from the data?' (CA Dept of Ed AI literacy table) — ai4k12.org

Kharashadzi et al., 'Chatbot application in a 5th grade science course' (2021, peer-reviewed): grade-5 students use an AI chatbot as a guide that supplements the teacher — useful, curiosity-raising, a partner for questions, not a replacement — pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8211302

NSTA + STAC, 'Sensemaking in the Age of AI' (2026): AI used 'purposefully and intentionally in service of student learning', in AI-resilient classrooms that 'preserve curiosity, productive struggle, and the habits of thinking'; science and engineering practices as the design frame for AI experiences

prep.title: The ledger briefing was already at home
prep.lead: Before class, the class met the addition-and-subtraction briefing — the market numbers and three home questions, at each student's own pace.
prep.goal: Recover the first exposure, so the ledger work begins with thinking — not with content delivery.
prep.pull: Now the probe: what does the class already hold about adding and subtracting?

diagnose.title: The gap map for the ledger office
diagnose.lead: Four checkpoints from the briefing. The class votes what it already holds — we are mapping gaps, not scoring students.
diagnose.goal: Build a gap map: what is known, and what is missing, before the bids are opened.
diagnose.pull: Knowledge building closes exactly what the map flags.

practice.title: Practice — feedback in seconds, not days
practice.lead: First with the model open, then with it closed, on the market lines. Every answer is met in the moment, not after a delayed correction.
practice.goal: Guided, then independent — learning happens at the moment of doing.
practice.pull: Now a genuinely new situation from the market. The critic arrives — as a critic, never as an author.

critic.title: A genuinely new situation from the market
critic.lead: The class produces its own work in a situation it has not seen before, then defends it. AI enters here — as a critic, never as an author.
critic.goal: Build the STEM production, transfer the method into new territory, and defend it through critique.
critic.pull: One individual task now decides each student's next path.

home: Take 298 + 57 in your head. Move the same small amount from one number to the other — what friendly pair do you make?
Why does 300 + 55 give the same total as 298 + 57? What moved, and where did it go?
Make your own line: pick a number one step from a round number and add a two-digit number. What is the checked total?

claims: I can add and subtract numbers within 1,000 with confidence.
I can round a number to the nearest ten or hundred quickly.
I can hold two steps in my head: move an amount, then take it back.
I can use the written column method as a check for a mental total.

independent.prompt: The next wet line: 404 + 39. What is the checked total?
independent.yes: Yes — give 4 to the 39 to make 43, take the 4 from the 404: 400 + 43 = 443.
independent.notYet: Not yet — move the same amount to make a friendly number, then take it back.

harder.prompt: A ledger line reads 997 + 165. Show the mental check: what friendly pair do you make, and what is the total?
harder.answer: Take 3 from the 165 to make the 997 a 1,000: 1,000 + 162 = 1,162.
harder.hint: The 997 is one step from a friendly number.

options.task: A 60-second mental-check presentation: your team picks the mental strategy (round both, adjust by the same amount), proves it live on three sealed ledger lines, and explains why the flagged line cannot stand.
options.stem: ask which line is off → plan the mental check → build the 60-second script → test it on three sealed lines before presenting → share it at the ledger desk

options.task: A catch-it sketch: the wet line, the mental check you ran, and the flag on the suspicious number. Draw the thinking arrow, not just the answer.
options.stem: ask which line to suspect → plan the sketch → run the mental check → test the flag against the exact sum → share it at the ledger desk

options.task: An AI-checked error hunt: build a ten-line mental-math worksheet for the class, then have the AI re-check every line. Where you and the AI disagree, settle it yourself and log the outcome.
options.stem: ask what a good error hunt looks like → plan the ten lines → build the worksheet → test it against the AI (settle every difference yourself) → share it on the wall

home: 5,218 + 2,874 — what is a reasonable total? Round each number to a friendly thousand and add the rounds.
Which total could never be right for 4,000 + 3,900: 7,900, 8,000 or 13,000? What catches the impossible one?
Estimate the cost of three things from the canteen menu before you add them. How close was your range?

claims: I can round numbers to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand.
I can add and subtract with friendly numbers in my head.
I can say which side of a rounded value a number sits on.
I can use an estimate to check whether an exact total is reasonable.

independent.prompt: The next cover lifts: 4,182 + 3,946. Which total is reasonable?
independent.yes: Yes — about 4,000 plus about 4,000 is about 8,000; the exact total must land near it.
independent.notYet: Not yet — round each number to a friendly thousand and add the rounds.

harder.prompt: A bid of 9,996 + 1,204. Estimate it, then find the exact total. How close was the estimate?
harder.answer: The estimate is 10,000 + 1,200 = 11,200 — and the exact total is 11,200, so the estimate landed exactly.
harder.hint: Round each number, add the rounds, then prove it.

options.task: An impossible-bid poster: take three sealed market bids, estimate each with a friendly-number range, and display the one impossible total with the range that catches it.
options.stem: ask which bid is impossible → plan the range (round to the thousand) → build the poster with all three estimates → test the range against the real totals → share it on the market wall

options.task: A bid map: place each sealed bid on a friendly-number line, show which bids land inside the possible range, and mark the impossible ones with the reason for rejection.
options.stem: ask where each bid could land → plan the range → estimate the totals → test each bid against the range → share it at the bid counter

options.task: A 60-second impossible-or-not verdict clip: ask the AI to propose three candidate bids, then judge each on camera — possible or impossible, with your estimate as the evidence. The AI supplies the bids; your verdicts are the work.
options.stem: ask what a possible bid looks like → plan the verdicts → request candidate bids from the AI (judge each one yourself) → test with friendly-number estimates → share it on the wall

home: 376 + 248 — estimate first, then add the columns. Does the exact total sit where the estimate predicted?
When do you have to trade in an addition — and where does the trade go?
Collect two real prices from home (a price tag, a receipt). Add them in columns and write the check beside the total.

claims: I can round numbers to a friendly value and use them to estimate.
I can add two-digit numbers with a trade.
I can line up columns by place value.
I can use addition to check an addition.

independent.prompt: The next receipt: 584 + 379. What is the checked total?
independent.yes: Yes — about 600 plus about 400 is about 1,000, and 963 sits just under it; the ones give 13, the tens 16, the hundreds 9.
independent.notYet: Not yet — estimate first, then add the columns and check the trades.

harder.prompt: Three receipts: 1,236 + 2,948 + 1,817. Add them, and write the check that proves the total.
harder.answer: 6,001 — the check: about 1,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 is about 6,000, and 6,001 sits right there.
harder.hint: Estimate all three first; add two, then the third.

options.task: A receipt-stack model: collect three real prices from the canteen menu, stack them in columns on paper strips, and build the desk model with the total and the check written beside it.
options.stem: ask what the class's own order really costs → collect three real prices (real data) → build the column stack → test it with the addition check → share the model at the ledger desk

options.task: A 90-second column-addition demo: add the market row on camera, then write the check beside the total. If the check fails, the video ends with you catching it yourself.
options.stem: ask what the row adds to → plan the demo → add column by column → test it with the addition check on camera → share the clip at the ledger desk

options.task: A 'we asked, we verified' poster from real canteen data: collect three real prices, add them yourself, then let the AI re-add independently — and show on the poster where you agreed, and whether the AI ever needed correcting.
options.stem: ask what the class's order costs → collect three real prices → add them yourself → test against the AI's independent re-add (correct it if it errs) → share it on the wall

home: 205,368 + 47,915 — estimate to the ten-thousand before adding. Where must the exact total land?
How many columns does the ledger need now, and how many did it need last week?
Add 138,427 + 69,584 in columns, then estimate first to see whether the total is reasonable.

claims: I can add multi-digit numbers with trades and check the total.
I can estimate a sum to the nearest thousand or ten-thousand.
I can line up numbers of different lengths by place value.
I can explain where an estimate must land before I compute.

independent.prompt: The next bundle: 284,936 + 127,058. What is the audited total?
independent.yes: Yes — about 280,000 plus about 130,000 is about 410,000, and 411,994 sits just past it.
independent.notYet: Not yet — estimate to the ten-thousand first, then add the columns from the right.

harder.prompt: The biggest bundle yet: 498,762 + 301,238. What is the total — and what is strange about it?
harder.answer: 800,000 — the two bundles make a round number, and the estimate proves it: about 500,000 + about 300,000 = 800,000.
harder.hint: Round each number — the estimate tells you the whole answer.

options.task: The ledger redesign: the old columns only hold four digits — design the new ledger page that carries seven-digit bundles without losing place value, and justify every column.
options.stem: ask what breaks in the old ledger → plan the new column layout → build the redesigned page → test it with the two biggest bundle totals → share the layout with the council

options.task: A before-and-after column sketch: the old page that could not hold the bundle, the redesigned page that can, with arrows on every new place and why it belongs there.
options.stem: ask why the old columns fail → plan the redesign → add the new places → test the bundle on the new page → share it at the ledger desk

options.task: A 60-second 'why the columns had to grow' talk: research one real seven-digit quantity with the AI — a city's population, a bridge's span in feet, your choice — verify it, and use it to show why the old page could not hold it.
options.stem: ask why the columns had to grow → plan the argument → research a real seven-digit quantity with the AI (verify it) → build the argument → test it against the redesigned page → share it on the wall

home: 725 − 348 — estimate first: about 700 minus about 350. Where must the exact difference land?
When the top digit is smaller than the bottom one, what must happen before you subtract?
Take 1,000 and subtract a three-digit number. Trade where you need to, and write the difference.

claims: I can add multi-digit numbers with trades and check them.
I can round a number and use it to estimate a difference.
I can subtract two-digit numbers with a trade.
I can use addition to check a subtraction.

independent.prompt: The reserve line: 903 − 457. What is the proven difference?
independent.yes: Yes — about 900 minus about 500 is about 400, and 446 sits just past it.
independent.notYet: Not yet — estimate first, then subtract the columns, trading where the top digit is smaller.

harder.prompt: The council spent 2,845 of a 5,000 reserve. Find the difference, then prove it with addition.
harder.hint: Add the difference back — if you land on the reserve, it is proved.

options.task: A reserve map: draw the council's money — the spend, the reserve, and the difference labelled on each segment — with the subtraction written beside the map.
options.stem: ask what is left after the spend → plan the map's segments → build the map with labelled values → test it: does spend + reserve equal the budget? → share it with the council

options.task: A 60-second 'the reserve, told honestly' recording: subtract the spend from the reserve on camera, then read the difference in the council's own words — what the reserve can and cannot cover.
options.stem: ask what is left → plan the recording → subtract → test the difference against the spend → share it at the council table

options.task: A paper reserve model with a real number: research one real council or school budget figure with the AI, verify it, then build the spend-reserve-difference model from your own paper strips.
options.stem: ask what the reserve must show → plan the model → research a real budget figure with the AI (verify it) → build the strips → test the subtraction → share it on the wall

home: 310,254 − 87,169 — estimate first. Where must the verified difference land?
Why is adding the difference back the strongest check on a subtraction?
Subtract 502,316 − 148,972 in columns, then prove the difference with addition.

claims: I can subtract multi-digit numbers with trades.
I can estimate a difference to the nearest thousand.
I can use addition to verify a subtraction.
I can keep the columns aligned when the numbers grow to six digits.

independent.prompt: The warehouse line: 483,912 − 167,458. What is the verified difference?
independent.yes: Yes — about 480,000 minus about 170,000 is about 310,000, and 316,454 sits just past it.
independent.notYet: Not yet — estimate first, then verify by adding the difference back.

harder.prompt: A ledger line shows 700,000 − 296,541 = 403,459. Is it verified? Show the check.
harder.answer: Verified: 403,459 + 296,541 = 700,000 exactly — the difference lands back on the reserve.
harder.hint: Add the difference to the spent — you must land on 700,000.

options.task: A 90-second verify-it video: film the warehouse subtraction, then the addition check that proves the difference — every trade visible on camera.
options.stem: ask how to prove a big difference → plan the two takes (subtract, then add to check) → build the clip → test it against the class's own copy → share it on the evidence wall

options.task: A subtract-then-check diagram: the subtraction on the left, the addition check on the right, and equal bars showing the two routes meet at the same number.
options.stem: ask how to prove the difference → plan the diagram → subtract → test it with the addition check → share it at the warehouse desk

options.task: A verification log: pick two subtractions from the ledger, solve them yourself, then let the AI check both independently. Record where you agreed, where you disagreed, and how you settled it.
options.stem: ask how to verify honestly → pick the two subtractions → solve them yourself → test against the AI's independent checks → share the log on the wall

home: 6,000 − 2,475 — the ones column must borrow, but the tens and hundreds are zeros. Where must the trade chain start?
What does 9,000 have to become before it can give to the ones?
Try 4,000 − 1,846 on paper. Draw an arrow for every trade you make.

claims: I can subtract multi-digit numbers with a single trade.
I can rename a number using place value (1 thousand = 10 hundreds).
I can use addition to verify a difference.
I can follow a trade chain across more than one place.

independent.prompt: The next damaged line: 9,000 − 3,268. What is the difference across the zeros?
independent.yes: Yes — the chain starts in the ones: 9,000 becomes 8,999 + 1, and 5,732 adds back exactly.
independent.notYet: Not yet — start the trade chain in the ones; the zeros must borrow from the left.

harder.prompt: Two lines crossed by zeros: 4,000 − 1,846 and 10,000 − 2,375. Find both differences and describe the chain each one needed.
harder.answer: 2,154 (one trade hop: thousands down to the ones) and 7,625 (a chain across three silent zeros).
harder.hint: Count the silent zeros between the place that can give and the one that must borrow.

options.task: An annotated trade drawing: redraw a water-damaged line crossed by zeros, and show every regrouping chain with labelled arrows — the silent zeros included.
options.stem: ask where the trade must start → plan the chain from the ones → build the drawing with arrows on every trade → test it by adding the difference back → share the annotated line

options.task: A cross-the-zero poster: the borrow chain from 6,000 − 2,475, every arrow labelled with what was borrowed and from where, so any reader can follow the chain.
options.stem: ask how the borrows travel → plan the chain → trace every regroup → test the chain against the difference → share it at the water-damaged page

options.task: A regrouping-path map for one subtraction from the real ledger: trace the borrows yourself, then let the AI challenge your path — if it finds an error, fix it yourself and show both routes on the map.
options.stem: ask where the borrows travel → plan the map → trace the path yourself → test it against the AI's challenge (fix it yourself) → share it on the wall

home: A polished answer can still hide a faulty step. What check catches the mistake even when the writing looks clean?
Budget 5,000; rows 2,340 and 1,875. Find the remainder, then prove it with addition.
Spot the error: a report claims 5,000 − 2,340 − 1,875 = 895. Run the check — what does it say?

claims: I can add and subtract multi-digit numbers and check both ways.
I can estimate a result before computing it.
I can explain each step of a computation in words.
I can separate a correct answer from the steps that produced it.

independent.prompt: A second budget card: 8,000; rows 3,412 and 2,968. What is the remainder?
independent.notYet: Not yet — take the rows off one at a time, then add all three back to the budget.

harder.prompt: The auditor's polished solution says the remainder is 1,720. Where does the faulty step hide, and what is the true remainder?
harder.answer: The true remainder is 1,620 — the polished 1,720 fails the addition check: 3,412 + 2,968 + 1,720 = 8,100, a hundred over the budget.
harder.hint: Run the check: rows + remainder must land exactly on 8,000.

wall.artifact: The sealed audit ledger and the class's one-page audit reports

options.task: The one-page audit report: the class receives a polished (but faulty) solution — produce the report with the finding, the faulty step, the corrected result, and the seal decision. This is the unit's final artifact.
options.stem: ask whether the polished answer stands → plan the audit (recompute, locate the faulty step) → build the one-page report → test the correction with the addition check → share it and issue the seal

options.task: The audit verdict read at the seal desk: 60 seconds to state the finding, the faulty step, the corrected result, and why the seal is issued or withheld. No notes after the first run.
options.stem: ask whether to sign → plan the verdict → critique the reasoning → test the correction against the check → share it at the seal desk

options.task: A 90-second auditor-versus-machine clip: you defend the polished solution on camera while the AI plays the critic — ask it to challenge, answer every challenge on camera yourself, and close with your seal decision.
options.stem: ask whether the reasoning survives → plan the clip → record the defence → let the AI challenge (answer every one yourself) → test the correction → share it on the wall
